meta.title: Langchain vs Llamaindex: Which one to choose in 2026? (models, context & API pricing & code compared)
meta.description: Compare Langchain and Llamaindex architectural trade-offs, context windows, model APIs, and integration, and review side-by-side TypeScript to choose the right stack.

verdict: Choose LangChain when you need broad orchestration: multi-step agents, tool calling, many model and vector-store integrations, and flexible chains across providers. Choose LlamaIndex when retrieval and indexing are the core problem: document parsing, chunking, hybrid search, query routing, and RAG evaluation. Many production teams use both, with LlamaIndex handling ingestion and retrieval and LangChain handling workflow logic. Validate current feature sets against your pinned version, since both frameworks change quickly.

comparison.toolA: LangChain is a general-purpose orchestration framework for LLM applications, built around composable runnable units, chains, tools, and agents. Its abstractions target workflows that combine prompts, models, retrievers, memory, and external tools, and the ecosystem includes LangGraph for stateful, graph-based agent workflows. The architecture favors flexibility, which means more design decisions fall to the developer.
comparison.toolB: LlamaIndex is a data framework focused on connecting LLMs to private and external data, with retrieval-augmented generation as its center of gravity. Its architecture centers on indexes, nodes, query engines, and retrievers, and it provides higher-level constructs for ingestion, parsing, and query routing. It also supports agents and workflows, but its abstractions are shaped primarily by data access patterns rather than general orchestration.

comparison.toolA: LangChain offers a mature retrieval layer with document loaders, text splitters, embedding integrations, vector-store wrappers, and retriever interfaces, plus patterns for multi-query and contextual compression. It covers standard RAG well and integrates with many external tools, but advanced retrieval pipelines often require more manual assembly. Exact retriever features depend on the integrations and package versions you use.
comparison.toolB: LlamaIndex is designed around RAG and provides richer out-of-the-box retrieval building blocks, including node-level metadata, multiple index types, hybrid and recursive retrieval, query engines, and response synthesizers. It also emphasizes structured ingestion of complex documents such as PDFs and offers evaluation utilities for retrieval quality. This makes it faster to reach a strong baseline on document-heavy question answering.

comparison.toolA: LangChain provides the most extensive agent tooling in this comparison, including tool-calling agents, structured output handling, and the separate LangGraph library for durable, stateful workflows with cycles and human-in-the-loop checkpoints. That breadth supports complex multi-agent and long-running processes, though it introduces more concepts to learn. Reliability still depends on model choice, prompt design, and careful testing.
comparison.toolB: LlamaIndex supports agents and event-driven workflows, and its agent capabilities have expanded, including tool use and multi-step reasoning over data. Its orchestration is generally simpler and better suited to data-centric pipelines than to highly branched agent graphs. For complex stateful agent systems, teams often pair it with a dedicated orchestration layer.

comparison.toolA: LangChain exposes many abstractions at once, and the ecosystem spans core libraries, integrations, LangGraph, and LangSmith, which can feel overwhelming to newcomers. Frequent releases have historically caused churn, so pinning versions and following current documentation matters. Developers with prior LLM experience generally find the composable model powerful once the core concepts click.
comparison.toolB: LlamaIndex tends to feel more approachable for retrieval-focused projects because its higher-level APIs deliver a working RAG pipeline with relatively little code. Its documentation is organized around data and query tasks, which matches common project goals. Projects that grow into general orchestration may eventually need additional structure.

comparison.toolA: LangChain maintains one of the broadest integration catalogs for chat models, embeddings, vector stores, document loaders, and third-party tools, and it benefits from a large community and abundant tutorials. The companion LangSmith product adds tracing and evaluation, with availability and limits depending on plan and configuration. Integration quality varies, so verify support for your specific provider and version.
comparison.toolB: LlamaIndex offers a substantial integration set covering major model providers, vector databases, and data sources, often with connectors tailored to ingestion. Its community is smaller than LangChain's, though active and growing. Coverage of niche providers or unusual data formats may lag behind LangChain's catalog in some cases.

comparison.toolA: LangChain integrates with LangSmith for tracing, evaluation datasets, and monitoring, and it also works with third-party observability platforms. These capabilities are valuable for debugging agent chains and comparing prompt versions, though some features are tied to paid tiers or specific configurations. Teams should confirm current pricing and feature availability before committing.
comparison.toolB: LlamaIndex includes evaluation modules for retrieval and response quality, such as faithfulness and relevance metrics, and it supports integration with external observability tools. Its evaluation focus is closely aligned with RAG quality, which is useful when tuning chunking and retrieval settings. Broader agent tracing typically relies on external platforms.

comparison.toolA: LangChain is largely a set of Python and JavaScript libraries, so runtime performance depends mostly on your model calls, vector store, and infrastructure rather than the framework itself. Abstraction layers add some overhead, which is usually minor relative to network and model latency. Deployment is flexible, and LangGraph supports durable execution for long-running workflows.
comparison.toolB: LlamaIndex follows a similar library-based deployment model, and its indexing and query abstractions are built for document-scale workloads. Performance depends on the chosen index type, embedding model, and storage backend, and caching and async patterns are available in current versions. Heavy ingestion jobs benefit from planning around batching and concurrency.

comparison.toolA: LangChain has a large user base and rapid release cadence, which drives fast feature growth but also means APIs can change between minor versions. The project has worked to stabilize core interfaces and separate concerns into packages, yet version pinning and regression testing remain prudent. Long-term maintenance is well supported by community and commercial backing.
comparison.toolB: LlamaIndex is actively developed with a strong focus on its data and retrieval niche, and its core abstractions have become more stable over time. It is smaller than LangChain in community size, so fewer third-party examples may exist for edge cases. Version pinning and reviewing changelogs are equally advisable here.

faq.q: Which framework should I choose for a document question-answering chatbot?
faq.a: LlamaIndex is usually the faster path for document question answering because its ingestion, indexing, and query-engine abstractions are built for exactly that workflow. It provides sensible defaults for parsing, chunking, and response synthesis, so you can reach a working prototype quickly. LangChain can also build this kind of chatbot, but you will typically assemble more pieces yourself. If your roadmap soon includes complex agents or many external tools, consider starting with LlamaIndex for retrieval and adding LangChain or LangGraph for orchestration.

faq.q: Is LangChain or LlamaIndex better for building autonomous agents?
faq.a: LangChain generally offers more extensive agent infrastructure, particularly through LangGraph, which supports stateful graphs, cycles, persistence, and human-in-the-loop checkpoints. That makes it better suited to complex, long-running agent workflows with branching logic. LlamaIndex supports agents and event-driven workflows, but its strengths are more concentrated in data access and retrieval. The right choice depends on how much orchestration complexity you expect; verify current agent features against your pinned versions, since both frameworks evolve quickly.

faq.q: Can I use LangChain and LlamaIndex together in one project?
faq.a: Yes, many teams combine them, often using LlamaIndex for ingestion, indexing, and retrieval while LangChain or LangGraph handles agent logic and workflow orchestration. Integration is feasible because both expose retriever and tool interfaces that can be adapted, though the exact glue code depends on the versions you use. Combining frameworks adds dependency and maintenance overhead, so document the integration points and keep versions pinned. For simpler projects, one framework is usually easier to maintain.

faq.q: Which framework has a gentler learning curve in 2026?
faq.a: LlamaIndex is often considered more approachable for retrieval-focused projects, because a functional RAG pipeline can be built with relatively few high-level calls. LangChain exposes more abstractions and a much larger integration surface, which can feel overwhelming at first, especially when agent and graph concepts are involved. That said, developers already familiar with LLM orchestration may find LangChain's composable model intuitive. The best way to judge is to prototype the same small task in both frameworks and compare the code you actually write.

faq.q: Do these frameworks lock me into a specific LLM provider or vector database?
faq.a: No, both are designed to be provider-agnostic and support many chat model, embedding, and vector-store integrations. You can generally swap providers by changing configuration or wrapper classes, though some features, such as tool calling or structured output, may behave differently across models. Integration coverage is not identical for every provider or database, so confirm support for your specific stack. Pinning versions helps avoid surprises when integration packages change.

faq.q: How do LangChain and LlamaIndex differ on evaluation and observability?
faq.a: LangChain pairs naturally with LangSmith for tracing, evaluation datasets, and monitoring of chains and agents, and it can also send traces to third-party observability platforms. LlamaIndex includes evaluation modules focused on retrieval and response quality, such as faithfulness and relevance metrics, alongside support for external observability tools. In practice, teams often add a dedicated evaluation or tracing service regardless of framework. Check current feature availability, plan limits, and any related costs before standardizing on a tool.

faq.q: Are these frameworks suitable for production systems?
faq.a: Both are used in production, but production readiness depends more on your architecture than on the framework alone. You will want version pinning, automated regression tests, tracing, fallback handling, and monitoring for latency and cost, and both frameworks can support these with the right configuration and integrations. Fast release cadences mean APIs can change, so treat upgrades as deliberate work. Start with a narrow proof of concept, measure quality, and expand only after the evaluation criteria are defined.

faq.q: Which framework is better for a small team with limited engineering time?
faq.a: For a small team whose main goal is search and question answering over private documents, LlamaIndex usually reduces the amount of custom code needed. For teams building multi-step tools, integrations across many services, or stateful agent workflows, LangChain's broader orchestration may save effort later despite the steeper start. A pragmatic approach is to prototype the core use case in one framework and avoid adopting both unless the integration clearly pays off. Keeping dependencies minimal is often the biggest maintenance win for small teams.
